57.title: The youngest son
57.hook: passing over his elder sons, Guru Ram Das names his youngest, Arjan, as the fifth Guru
57.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Guru Arjan as the fifth Guru, chosen by his father, Guru Ram Das; the story of his choosing is told as another sign that the Guruship went to the one most devoted, not the one first in line.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lavan, four rounds around the scripture. Your line was four rounds, one life.

At a family dinner there's the one who talks first, and the one who mostly listens. Guru Ram Das and Bibi Bhani had three sons. The eldest, Prithi Chand, was capable and ambitious, and managed much of the growing community's practical business. Tradition says he fully expected to be the next Guru. The middle son, Mahadev, was gentle and withdrawn, and seemed to want nothing to do with worldly affairs. And the youngest was Arjan: quiet, devoted, still a young man.
screen: `THE ONE WHO TALKS FIRST.` → `PRITHI CHAND, MAHADEV, ARJAN.` → `THE YOUNGEST, STILL A YOUNG MAN.`

segments.voice: Guru Ram Das chose Arjan. Tradition dates it to 1581, when Arjan was about eighteen. It made Prithi Chand bitterly angry; more on that in a couple of days. Why Arjan? Sikh tradition tells of a test. The Guru needed someone to go to Lahore, to represent the family at a relative's wedding, and to stay there until he was called back. Prithi Chand found a reason not to go; he didn't want to be far away while the succession was being decided. Mahadev wasn't interested. Arjan simply went, and waited, far from home, for a very long time. What happened while he waited is tomorrow's story. For today, look at the pattern; it has come up on this path before. Guru Nanak passed over his own sons for Lehna, the man who carried the wet grass. Guru Angad chose the old water carrier. Guru Amar Das chose the orphan with the tray of grams. Now Guru Ram Das passes over the confident eldest son for the quiet youngest. Each time, the one who was ready wasn't the one who pushed forward. It was the one who served, and waited, and didn't make the moment about himself. One thing changes here: from now on, the Guruship stays in Guru Ram Das's family. The rule doesn't: not the eldest, not the loudest, but the one who is ready. And with that choice, Guru Ram Das's part of the story closes: the orphan, the pool, the four rounds, the youngest son.

Hold their face in mind, and think what they'd do if someone trusted them with more.

58.title: Letters from Lahore
58.hook: sent away as a young man, Arjan writes longing letters to his father in verse (Majh, ang 96)
58.howItsDone: The Shabad Hazare, Guru Arjan's four verses of longing from Lahore, are in the Guru Granth Sahib in raga Majh, and some Sikhs include them in their morning prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Arjan, the youngest son, chosen to be the fifth Guru. Your line was the quiet one was ready.

Have you ever written to someone you love, far away, and waited, and heard nothing back? Every few minutes, checking. Nothing. Young Arjan is in Lahore. His father sent him there and told him to stay until he was called. So he stayed. Weeks went by. Months. No word came. He missed his father, who was also his teacher, his Guru. So he wrote a letter. Not in prose. In verse.
screen: `A MESSAGE, AND NO REPLY.` → `ARJAN WAITS IN LAHORE.` → `HE WRITES TO HIS FATHER, IN VERSE.`

segments.voice: The letter was a short hymn, now in the scripture, in raga Majh. Its first line says, in paraphrase: my mind longs for a sight of the Guru. It cries out like the rainbird, the chatrik, which in Indian poetry waits and calls for the one raindrop it will drink. My thirst isn't quenched, the verse says; I can't find peace without the sight of my beloved. He sent it. No reply. He wrote a second verse, even more aching: it has been so long since he saw his beloved's face. Still nothing. Here's what tradition says was happening. His eldest brother, Prithi Chand, was intercepting the letters; he didn't want Arjan anywhere near their father while the succession was open. So when Arjan wrote a third, which says a single moment apart feels like the dark age, he marked it with a number: three. That letter reached Guru Ram Das. The Guru saw the three, asked about the first two, found out what had happened, and sent for Arjan at once. When they met again, Arjan sang a fourth verse, the joy of reunion, and together the four make one hymn. Sikhs call it the Shabad Hazare, and some include it in their morning prayers. Two things stand out. Longing isn't treated as weakness here: the Gurus' hymns use the language of missing someone for the soul missing God, and in this hymn, missing a father and missing God are sung as one ache. And tradition tells the waiting as the test. Arjan never stopped writing, and he never stopped waiting.

59.title: A jealous brother
59.hook: his elder brother Prithi Chand resents him and makes trouble for years
59.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Prithi Chand's rivalry as a hard chapter in Guru Arjan's life, and read Guru Arjan's hymns of protection and trust in God, some sung in daily prayers, with those years in mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shabad Hazare, and a third letter with a number on it. Your line was my mind longs.

Who got the bigger room. Who Dad liked more. Some arguments outlive the house they started in, and a holiday dinner turns into careful choices about where people sit. The Bible tells stories like this too: Cain and Abel, Joseph and his brothers. The Sikh story has one. Arjan was now the fifth Guru, and his eldest brother, Prithi Chand, the one who intercepted the letters, did not accept it. Tradition says he never did.
screen: `WHO DAD LIKED MORE.` → `CAIN AND ABEL, JOSEPH'S BROTHERS.` → `PRITHI CHAND DOES NOT ACCEPT IT.`

segments.voice: Prithi Chand set himself up as a rival Guru. Tradition says he gathered his own followers and collected offerings meant for the Guru's kitchen, so that for a while the langar at Amritsar ran short. He even wrote hymns of his own signed with the name Nanak, as if they were the Gurus' words. Bhai Gurdas, the Sikh poet, gave his followers a sharp name: minas, the deceivers. Tradition tells darker stories too, of attempts to harm Guru Arjan's young son, Hargobind: a nurse with poison, a snake, a poisoned dish. Each time, the stories say, the child was spared. So how did Guru Arjan respond? He didn't raise an army against his brother. He didn't curse him. He kept doing his work: building, singing, serving the community. And he trusted his son's life to God. The scripture holds hymns of Guru Arjan's full of gratitude for protection. In one, he says, in paraphrase, that the hot wind cannot touch the one who is under God's shelter. Sikh tradition links some of them to those years. So the line, pray for the difficult one, doesn't mean pretending it's fine. The offerings really go missing; the child is really in danger. What the Guru refuses is to become like his brother. He leaves him to God and keeps his own work going: a Guru, and still a brother, across the table from someone who wanted his place.

Let the person's face be there, and notice what happens in your chest. If you pray, hold them before God in whatever words you use; if you don't, just wish them one good thing.

60.title: The house with four doors
60.hook: Guru Arjan builds the Harmandir Sahib low in the pool with doors on four sides, open to all
60.howItsDone: The Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar is the holiest gurdwara for Sikhs; visitors of every faith cover their heads, walk down into the complex, circle the pool, and eat together in its langar, which serves people day and night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Prithi Chand, and a Guru who answered with work, not revenge. Your line was pray for the difficult one.

Think about how important buildings are usually designed. They sit up high, on a hill or a platform, with a grand staircase and one main entrance, maybe with a guard. The meaning is clear: this place is above you, and you come in by permission, through the front. Now picture the pool at Amritsar that Guru Ram Das began. His son, Guru Arjan, finished it, and in the middle of the water he began to build a house of God. Almost every choice he made about that building turns the usual meaning upside down.
screen: `HIGH UP, ONE GRAND ENTRANCE.` → `THE POOL AT AMRITSAR.` → `A HOUSE IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WATER.`

segments.voice: It's called the Harmandir Sahib. Hari is a name for God, mandir means temple or house, and Sahib is a word of respect: the house of God. Many people know it as the Golden Temple, for the gold that covers it; that came much later, in the nineteenth century. First, instead of raising it high, Guru Arjan set it low. You walk down steps to reach it, so everyone who enters, rich or poor, comes down a little. Humility, built into the architecture. Second, instead of one grand entrance, he gave it doors on all four sides. In a world that sorted people by caste and by creed, this house was open from every direction, to everyone. Remember Guru Nanak's feet toward the Kaaba, and the question: which way is God not? Here's that question turned into a building. Tradition adds one more detail. Many Sikhs say the foundation stone was laid by a Muslim Sufi, Mian Mir, a friend of the Guru's from Lahore. Historians debate that story, but it has been told for a very long time, and it fits the house. The building was finished around 1604. It stands in the middle of the pool, reached by a causeway, and to this day the langar there feeds tens of thousands of people every day, of every faith and none. What Guru Arjan placed at its center is the story of the next few days.
screen: `HARMANDIR — THE HOUSE OF GOD.` · `SET LOW: YOU WALK DOWN TO ENTER.` · `FOUR DOORS, FOR EVERY DIRECTION.` · `A FOUNDATION STONE, TRADITION SAYS.` · then, large: `OPEN ON EVERY SIDE.`

segments.voice: If you can, get up and open a door, your front door, a window, the door to your room, and stand in it a moment, feeling the air come through. Think of who you'd welcome through it, and who you might have kept out without meaning to. Leave it open a while, if it's safe.
Harmandir Sahib. The house of God at Amritsar, set low in the pool with doors on four sides, open to all. Today's word.
Your line: open on every side. Four doors, one house, set low in the water. That's sixty days.

61.title: Gathering the hymns
61.hook: with Bhai Gurdas as scribe, he gathers the Gurus' hymns and those of other saints into one book
61.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Guru Arjan as the compiler of the Adi Granth, the book that became the Guru Granth Sahib, and the hymns of Kabir, Namdev, Ravidas, Farid and other saints are sung in gurdwaras alongside the Gurus' own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Harmandir Sahib: built low, with a door on every side. Your line was open on every side.

A grandmother's lullaby. The hymn at every funeral. The tune someone hums in the kitchen. Songs like these often live only in people, and when the people go, verses slip away, words drift, and sometimes someone adds a verse of their own and passes it off as the old one. By the time of Guru Arjan, the Sikh community had four Gurus' worth of hymns, sung every day, copied in handwritten books kept by different families. And tradition says others were writing hymns in Guru Nanak's name that he never wrote. Guru Arjan decided the words needed one home.
screen: `SONGS THAT LIVE IN PEOPLE.` → `FOUR GURUS' WORTH OF HYMNS.` → `ONE HOME FOR THE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Tradition says that around 1603, at a quiet spot by a pool near Amritsar, Guru Arjan sat down to make a book. His scribe was Bhai Gurdas, a scholar and poet, the Guru's relative, whose own verses Sikhs still read. The Guru dictated; Bhai Gurdas wrote. First, he gathered. Earlier Gurus' hymns had been collected in handwritten volumes under the third Guru, and tradition says those books were kept by his son, Baba Mohan, who would not hand them over. So Guru Arjan went to his house and sang outside his window, a hymn in his honor, until Mohan came down and gave them up. Second, he sorted: not by author or by date, but by raga, the musical mode each hymn was meant to be sung in, so the book is laid out like a songbook for the day and its moods. Third, the surprise: he opened the book to others. Beside the Gurus' words he placed hymns by saints from outside the Sikh community: Kabir, a weaver from Benares; Namdev, a calico printer; Ravidas, a leatherworker whom his society called untouchable; and Sheikh Farid, a Muslim Sufi who had lived centuries before. Hindu and Muslim, high caste and low, on the same pages; Sikhs understand it as the Guru hearing in them the same truth about the one God. And he left some things out: the hymns written falsely in Nanak's name did not go in. Gather, sort, open the pages, and guard them. That's how a scattered songbook became one book.
screen: `GURU ARJAN DICTATES, BHAI GURDAS WRITES.` · `SINGING FOR THE OLD BOOKS.` · `SORTED BY RAGA, LIKE A SONGBOOK.` · `KABIR, RAVIDAS, FARID ON ONE PAGE.` · then, large: `ONE HOME FOR THE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Let your mind go looking, the way the Guru went looking: a line someone said that you've never forgotten, a recipe only one person in your family knows, a song, a joke, a piece of advice. Pick one, and picture where it lives right now: in one person's head, on a scrap of paper, in a phone that could break. Hold it a while, and ask where it would be safe.

Your line: gather what is true. Tomorrow, the gathered book finds its place. Sixty-one days in.

62.title: The Adi Granth installed, 1604
62.hook: the book is placed in the Harmandir and Baba Buddha reads the first hukam
62.howItsDone: Every day in gurdwaras, the Guru Granth Sahib is opened and a hymn read at random as the hukam, the day's word; the hukam from the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar is shared widely each morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, raag, and gathering the hymns: Guru Arjan and Bhai Gurdas made one book. Your line was gather what is true.

The book is finished. Page after page, written by hand, every hymn set under its raga. Now what? You could put it on a shelf, or keep it in the Guru's own room. Guru Arjan did neither. In 1604 the book was carried in procession to the Harmandir Sahib, the house with four doors in the middle of the pool. Tradition says the old man Baba Buddha, who had known Guru Nanak as a boy, carried it on his head, and the Guru walked behind with a whisk, waving it over the book the way you'd honor a king.
screen: `THE BOOK IS FINISHED.` → `CARRIED ON BABA BUDDHA'S HEAD.` → `THE GURU WALKS BEHIND.`

segments.voice: Adi means first, or original. Granth means book. The first book: that's what Sikhs call the volume Guru Arjan compiled. Much later it would become the Guru Granth Sahib, a story for another day. Now watch what happens in the Harmandir. The book is placed on a raised seat in the center, under a canopy, and the Guru sits below it. The man who made it takes a humbler place than the words. Baba Buddha is named the first granthi, the keeper and reader of the book. Then comes a moment Sikhs still repeat each day. He opens the book at random and reads the hymn at the top of the left page. That reading is called a hukam, an order, or a word for the day. Tradition says the very first hukam was a line of Guru Arjan's own, saying in plain words that God himself stands up to carry out the work of the saints. A fitting word for a new house. The practice goes on in gurdwaras all over the world: every morning the book is opened, and a random hymn is read as the word for the day. Some Sikhs look up the Harmandir Sahib's hukam on their phones before breakfast. A practice from 1604, in your pocket. The words were gathered, sorted and guarded. Now they have a home, a keeper, and a voice.

63.title: Arrest at Lahore
63.hook: summoned by the emperor Jahangir's order, Guru Arjan is imprisoned and tortured in the heat of Lahore
63.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Arjan's imprisonment and torture in Lahore in the hymns, sermons and stories of his martyrdom anniversary each summer, and the site in Lahore is marked by Gurdwara Dera Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Adi Granth: carried into the Harmandir, with the Guru seated below it. Your line was the word has a home.

Come to Lahore. In 1605 a new emperor, Jahangir, takes the Mughal throne, and within a year his order reaches Guru Arjan. It is early summer on the plains of Punjab, the hottest time of the year. Look at the week behind him: a quiet youngest son chosen as Guru, letters of longing from Lahore, a jealous brother, a house with four doors, a book gathered from many voices and given a home. The Guru has built a great deal in a short time. Crowds come to Amritsar. The community is growing, organized, confident, and people are noticing. The week that began in longing for Lahore ends there.
screen: `COME TO LAHORE.` → `A NEW EMPEROR, JAHANGIR.` → `A WEEK OF BUILDING.`

segments.voice: Why was the Guru arrested? The sources give more than one answer, and historians weigh them differently. Jahangir left a memoir, and in it he writes about the Guru with open irritation: too many people, Hindus and Muslims both, were following him, and the emperor wanted it stopped. There was politics too. Jahangir's son, Prince Khusrau, had rebelled, and the memoir itself says the prince stopped to see the Guru on his way; the Sikh accounts say the Guru blessed him, as he blessed anyone who came. And Sikh tradition adds a court official, Chandu Shah, with a personal grudge. What the Sikh accounts agree on is what came next. The Guru was held in Lahore, and in the summer heat he was tortured. Tradition remembers it in terrible detail: made to sit on a red-hot iron plate, with burning sand poured over him. I won't linger there. What Sikhs linger on is how he sat. A friend came: Mian Mir, a Muslim Sufi saint of Lahore, whom tradition remembers as close to the Guru. Horrified, he offered to go to the emperor and plead. Tradition says the Guru calmly told him not to: this too was within God's will, and he would bear it. In the Sikh accounts he did not shout, and did not curse the emperor. He sat, stayed steady, and kept remembering. Simran, the word from day fourteen, is doing its hardest work here. Tomorrow, how it ended, and what Sikhs call him because of it.
screen: `WHY? MORE THAN ONE ANSWER.` · `HELD IN THE HEAT OF LAHORE.` · `MIAN MIR OFFERS TO PLEAD.` · `STEADY, AND REMEMBERING.` · then, large: `STEADY IN THE HEAT.`

segments.voice: Sit still for one minute, then a little longer: hands in your lap, feet on the floor, nothing to fix and nothing to answer. When something wants you to move, an itch, a thought, a sound, don't fight it and don't follow it; stay. If you remember a name for God, let it ride on your breath; if not, let the breath be your anchor.
Simran. Remembering God's name, the practice Guru Arjan kept while tortured in the summer heat at Lahore, staying steady and unshouting.
Your line: steady in the heat. Thank you for sitting with a hard story. Day sixty-three, and another week behind you.
